quote_text: The only way of discovering the limits of the possible is to venture a little way past them into the impossible.
idea_text: A kettle that tells you what your water is made of.
Scoville strips on restaurant menus.
A résumé that ships as a container image.
Textbooks that print their own errata.
Noise-cancelling, but for smell.
Rentable thermal mass.
A citation half-life badge on arXiv.
A regret button at checkout.
A hostel-scale pressure-cook-and-seal machine.
Receipts that print water footprint beside the price.
idea_prompt: Ten products that should exist but don't

quote_text: I have had my results for a long time: but I do not yet know how I am to arrive at them.
idea_text: A bonded claim registry: publish a fact, stake money against it.
Source-quality scoring for answer engines, published monthly.
Reverse SEO: getting a person's name *out* of model outputs.
A robots.txt licensing broker for publishers under 100k readers.
Stringers-for-hire who go physically verify one fact.
Structured-claim hosting: your facts, emitted for retrieval, not for reading.
Competitive intelligence on which fake sites recommend your rival.
Errors-and-omissions insurance for purchases made on an AI recommendation.
A domain-age and template-similarity API, sold as one boolean.
Print-only publishing for things that must stay uncrawlable.
idea_prompt: Ten businesses that only make sense now that machines, not people, read the web

quote_text: He hoped and prayed that there wasn't an afterlife. Then he realized there was a contradiction involved here and merely hoped that there wasn't an afterlife.
idea_text: A seat-swap board at the station, so groups travelling apart can trade into one bay.
Sleeper-class curtains that actually close, sold as a ten-rupee clip you carry in your bag.
A regional snack subscription that meets you on the platform at whichever junction you pass at dinnertime.
Route-timed audio: a two-hour story that ends exactly as you pull into your station.
A window seat rated by what is outside it, not by legroom.
A one-page paper newspaper printed for that specific train, that morning.
Compartment-sized board games with magnetic pieces and no small parts to lose.
A shared playlist per coach that anyone aboard can add one song to.
Left-luggage lockers at the arrival station booked from the train, so you can walk out and go straight somewhere.
Something that puts randomness back into what you watch or read on a long journey.
idea_prompt: Ten ways to make a long train journey something you look forward to

quote_text: Almost all absurdity of conduct arises from the imitation of those whom we cannot resemble.
idea_text: A gym that locks the door behind you for a full hour.
A courier that is proudly slow and guarantees your parcel arrives on the day you actually need it, not before.
A phone plan that gets more expensive the more you use it.
A shop that stocks exactly one of everything and never restocks.
A newspaper printed a week late.
A subscription whose only job is to cancel your other subscriptions.
A hotel with no windows, no clock and no wifi, sold as the best sleep of your life.
Quiet rooms in malls and stations, rented by the ten minutes.
A moving company that throws away a third of your things, chosen by you before packing day.
A neighbourhood noticeboard that charges local traders nothing and refuses to expand past one postcode.
idea_prompt: Ten terrible business ideas that would somehow still work

quote_text: When you want to know how things really work, study them when they're coming apart.
idea_text: A repair counter for exactly one category of thing — zips, and nothing else.
A room where you rent the tool you need for one afternoon and give it back the same day.
A photographer who only does the boring compulsory photographs: passports, visas, insurance claims, house inventories.
A one-room laundry that specialises in things other laundries refuse: sarees, jerseys, curtains, toys.
Assembly-as-a-service for flat-pack furniture, bought by the hour.
A shop that scans and returns your old photo albums, letters and VHS tapes, then throws nothing away.
A weekend STEAM class run out of a spare room for homeschooled kids in one neighbourhood.
A cash-only tailoring desk inside a gym, altering clothes that no longer fit.
A service that sits with elderly people for two hours a week and does whatever the phone requires: forms, bills, appointments, banks.
A verified-purchase-only review desk for one product category, funded by shoppers rather than sellers.
idea_prompt: Ten small businesses you could run out of a single room

quote_text: The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.
idea_text: Ride one city bus route from its first stop to its last, then get off wherever it looked most interesting on the way out.
Do the one small task you have been avoiding for months, then spend the rest of the day insufferably pleased with yourself.
Cook something from a state you have never visited, buying only what a single neighbourhood market can supply.
Walk for two hours with a 1940s radio serial in your ears instead of music.
Eat the second-cheapest thing on the menu at five different places instead of one proper meal at one.
Find the oldest building within walking distance, read everything you can about it, and only then go and stand in front of it.
Sit in a park for an hour with paper and write down every distinct sound you hear.
Photograph the same street corner once an hour from sunrise to sunset.
Walk into a shop for a hobby you do not have and ask the owner what beginners always get wrong.
Take a friend somewhere neither of you has been and let them choose the direction at every junction.
idea_prompt: Ten things to do with a free Sunday and ₹500
